extracted.subtask_description: Practical craft advice for fiction writers about mindset, workspace, descriptive technique, and the fundamental 'tools' of prose (vocabulary, voice, reading). Emphases include how to approach the blank page, how to build a personal toolbox, and how to communicate images to readers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Writing is telepathy
rubrics_metrics.description: Writing is an act of telepathy: the writer must transmit images, scenes, and feelings so readers receive the same mental picture (King's rabbit/cage/blue-eight example).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aim to create clear, shareable mental images; use evocative details that most readers can map to their own experience so a meeting of the minds occurs. Avoid needless obscurity; it's the successful transmission — not authorial cleverness — that matters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not come lightly to the blank page
rubrics_metrics.description: You must not come lightly to the blank page — take writing seriously and treat the work with commitment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This doesn't mean reverence or self-censorship: bring seriousness of purpose but retain humor and individuality. Writing is not a popularity contest, moral Olympics, or church; if you cannot take the craft seriously, you should do something else.

rubrics_metrics.name: Life supports art; keep your desk in the corner
rubrics_metrics.description: Life isn't a support-system for art. It's the other way around — practical balance between living and writing matters; King recommends placing your desk in the corner rather than centering it in the room.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Physically locating your desk in the corner is a mnemonic and practical reminder to prioritize life (family, health) while practicing your craft. Don't let writing become an all-consuming altar that ruins the life it should be serving.

rubrics_metrics.name: Have a far-seeing/receiving place (favorite writing spot)
rubrics_metrics.description: Create a personal 'far-seeing' place — a preferred physical spot (chair, couch, study) with good light and a strong vibe where you do your best reading and writing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A consistent place helps focus telepathic transmission and reception. Books are portable magic, but cultivating a regular workspace or seat strengthens habit and concentration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use evocative, rough comparisons rather than prissy precision
rubrics_metrics.description: Prefer evocative, rough comparisons to over-precise, manual-like descriptions; exact measurements and hyper-specific technical detail can turn prose into an instruction manual and sap the fun.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Give the reader enough to visualize (a red tablecloth, a see-through cage, an eight on a rabbit) without enumerating dimensions or irrelevant material details. Allow room for reader interpretation and variation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Construct and carry a writing toolbox
rubrics_metrics.description: Build a metaphorical toolbox of writing tools (techniques, habits, skills) and develop the muscle to carry it with you so you're prepared for unexpected jobs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make the toolbox portable and practical; King recommends at least four levels (not so big it becomes unportable). Think about organization (common tools on top, little drawers for specifics) and tailor contents to your needs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Common tools go on top; vocabulary is the bread of writing
rubrics_metrics.description: Place the commonest tools where they're easiest to access. Chief among these is vocabulary — 'the bread of writing.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: You may happily use whatever vocabulary you already have; quality of use matters more than size. Don't obsess about acquiring long words for their own sake; use words well and economically.

rubrics_metrics.name: Don't dress up vocabulary with needlessly long or pretentious words
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid substituting long, fancy words for simple, direct ones (e.g., 'emolument' vs. 'tip', 'perform an act of excretion' vs. 'take a shit').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pretentious diction embarrasses the writing. Choose plain words that do the job and fit your voice and audience. If crude plain language would offend your audience, choose a simple polite alternative — but don't inflate language to sound learned.

rubrics_metrics.name: Let vocabulary grow naturally by reading — don't force improvement
rubrics_metrics.description: You will improve your vocabulary and command of language primarily by reading; don't make a conscious, self-conscious effort to 'dress up' your prose.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Read widely and deliberately (King notes unabridged audiobooks as a preference for listening). Exposure to good writing will expand your usable vocabulary over time; act on that growth rather than forcing novelty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maintain and clean your tools (revisit rusty skills)
rubrics_metrics.description: Regularly inspect the tools in your toolbox, remind yourself of their functions, and clean off any that have become rusty from disuse.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Skills atrophy if unused; revisit fundamentals, refresh rusty techniques, and make sure your toolkit remains ready for use so you don't become discouraged at a task.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use voice-appropriate and register-appropriate language
rubrics_metrics.description: Choose vocabulary, dialect, and phonetic rendering that fit the characters and tone (e.g., Tom Wolfe's street phonetics, Elmore Leonard's ear for dialogue).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authentic voice can require nonstandard spellings or slang; when used skillfully it enriches the page. Know when to translate vernacular to readable phonetics and when to keep language simple for clarity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Keep your toolbox a manageable size (portability over completeness)
rubrics_metrics.description: A toolbox with too many levels or too many tools becomes unwieldy and loses its chief virtue: portability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Balance the number and complexity of tools with the need to carry them into actual writing situations. Prioritize essential, frequently used tools so you can reach for them quickly and use them without getting bogged down.
